title: Peeking Iterator
statement:
Write a class `PeekingIterator` that wraps an existing iterator of integers and adds a way to look at the upcoming value without using it up.

- `new PeekingIterator(iterator)` receives the iterator to wrap. It is an object with exactly two methods: `iterator.hasNext()` tells whether it still has a value, and `iterator.next()` hands out its next value and moves past it. It cannot be indexed and does not reveal its length. (The TypeScript starter types it as `number[]` only because the signature format has no iterator type; it is still this object.)
- `next()` returns the upcoming value and moves past it.
- `hasNext()` returns `true` while some value has not been returned by `next()` yet, and `false` afterwards.
- `peek()` returns the upcoming value **without** moving past it, so the following `peek()` or `next()` gives the same value.

`next()` and `peek()` are only called when a value remains. Each case uses the design format `[operations, arguments]`: the first operation is `"PeekingIterator"`, whose argument is the list of values the wrapped iterator produces (the judge turns it into the iterator object above), and the answer lists every call's result, with `null` for the constructor.
constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 1000 (the values behind the wrapped iterator)
Every call to next and peek happens while a value remains
At most 1000 calls are made to next, hasNext and peek
notes:
## Intuition

The wrapped iterator can only hand out a value by consuming it. To show the upcoming value without losing it, take it out once and keep it in a one-value cache until `next()` asks for it. A simple alternative copies every value into an array in the constructor and walks an index, but that reads the whole iterator up front and uses O(n) memory; the cache needs only one slot and reads values only when asked.

## Approach

1. Store the wrapped `iterator`, a flag `hasPeeked` (is a value cached?) and the cached value `peeked`.
2. `peek()`: if nothing is cached, pull one value from `iterator.next()` into `peeked` and set `hasPeeked`. Return `peeked`.
3. `next()`: if a value is cached, clear the flag and return it; otherwise pass the call straight to `iterator.next()`.
4. `hasNext()`: a value remains if one is cached or the wrapped iterator still has one.

## Example 1, step by step

The wrapped iterator yields `1, 2, 3`.

- `next()`: nothing is cached, so it returns `iterator.next()`, which is `1`.
- `peek()`: nothing cached; it pulls `2` into `peeked`, sets `hasPeeked = true` and returns `2`.
- `next()`: `hasPeeked` is true, so it clears the flag and returns the cached `2`.
- `next()`: nothing cached; it returns `iterator.next()`, which is `3`.
- `hasNext()`: no cached value and the wrapped iterator is empty, so `false`.

Results: `[null, 1, 2, 2, 3, false]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) for every call; each value is pulled from the wrapped iterator exactly once.
- Space: O(1): one cached value and a flag.

## Pitfalls

- `hasNext()` must also check the cache: after peeking the last value the wrapped iterator is empty, yet a value remains.
- Repeated `peek()` calls must not pull new values; only fill the cache when it is empty.
- Use a separate flag instead of a sentinel such as `null` or `0`, so the design still works when the values are of any type (the follow-up asks for a generic version).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `iterator` | the wrapped iterator with `hasNext()` and `next()` |
| `hasPeeked` | whether a value has been taken out and not yet returned by `next()` |
| `peeked` | that cached value |
